edits.english: It is stated in the mishna: This is the principle: Anything that benefits from a forbidden item imparting a beneficial flavor to it is forbidden, and anything that does not benefit from a forbidden item imparting flavor to it is permitted, e.g., forbidden vinegar that fell onto split beans, as the flavor imparted by the vinegar does not enhance the taste of the beans. Rav Yehuda says that Shmuel says: This is the halakha.

edits.hebrew: הכי הלכתא: דנותן טעם לפגם מותר.

edits.english: A We learned in the Mishna: This is the principle: Anything that benefits by imparting a beneficial flavor is forbidden. But anything that imparts a detrimental flavor, such as forbidden vinegar in split beans, does not forbid. Rav Yehuda says that Shmuel says: This is the halakha.

The Rishonim wrote that it was necessary to rule according to this view (even though it is an anonymous Mishna, and usually the halakha follows an anonymous Mishna, and especially since no one disputes this opinion in our Mishna) because the reasoning of Rabbi Meir, who forbids even a detrimental flavor in a Braittha below (page 2), is plausible. See below regarding this matter.

And similarly, vinegar that fell into split beans: It is difficult, for have we not been taught until now that imparting a detrimental flavor is permitted? We learn this from the beginning of the Mishna. And it can be said that it comes to teach us that even though when it falls into cold split beans it improves them, as stated in the Gemara, nevertheless, into hot split beans it is permitted, for we do not issue a decree because of cold ones.

Rav Yehuda says that Shmuel says: This is the halakha: This is how it is written in the books, and it also appears from what is said nearby: 'From the words of all of them we learn that imparting a detrimental flavor is permitted.' And what does 'from the words of all of them' mean? Is it because we explain the Mishna that they hold this opinion? Rather, since it is taught 'This is the halakha,' let us say that we learn explicitly from Rabbi Yehuda, and also explicitly from Rabbi Yochanan nearby, who says: 'If one added, imparting a detrimental flavor is permitted.' And presumably, Rabba bar bar Ḥana and Rav (Idi), who came to explain the Mishna, also follow their opinion.

And Rav Yehuda says that Shmuel says: The Sages taught this only with regard to a case where the vinegar fell into hot split beans, imparting flavor to their detriment. But if the vinegar fell into cold split beans, the vinegar enhances the flavor, and if a person subsequently heated them, it becomes like a dish that some added ingredient first enhanced its flavor and ultimately detracted from it, and it is rendered forbidden, as the initial flavor that was imparted was beneficial.
Vinegar imparts a detrimental flavor to hot split beans and improves cold ones.
And one heated them: Over the fire after the vinegar fell into them.

Wine vinegar of an idolater that fell into hot split beans imparts a detrimental flavor, and they are permitted. But if it fell into cold ones, it improves them and they are forbidden, even if one heated them afterwards and they reverted to having a detrimental flavor. NOTE: And regarding spices that absorbed libation wine and were put into a dish, if there are sixty parts against the wine absorbed in them, everything is permitted, even though spices are made for flavor, since they are not forbidden on their own, they are nullified. And if the wine in them imparts a detrimental flavor to the dish, even sixty parts are not needed (Beit Yosef in the name of Rashba).

A detrimental flavor does not need to be so disgusting that one stops eating it; even if it is only slightly detrimental, it does not forbid the mixture. Some say this applies specifically when a small amount of a forbidden item is mixed with a large amount of a permitted item. However, if a large amount of a forbidden item is mixed with a small amount of a permitted item, or even if it is half and half, we do not say that “imparting a detrimental flavor is permissible” until it makes the mixture completely unfit for human consumption. If there are no substantial pieces of the forbidden item, but only its taste, even if there is a large amount of the forbidden item and a small amount of the permitted item, it is permitted if it is only slightly detrimental. And there is one who ḥokhekh (meaning, this posek tends to be stringent and forbids) to say that if the forbidden item has increased the quantity of the permitted item such that it is more beneficial when eaten in its increased quantity than it is detrimental in its diminished flavor, it is forbidden until it becomes unfit for human consumption. To what cases do these words apply? To those where the flavor is detrimental from beginning to end. But if it initially improved the flavor and ultimately detracted from it, or if it was initially detrimental and ultimately improved it, these items are forbidden. NOTE: There are those who say that even though the forbidden item imparts a detrimental taste and the food is permitted, the pot itself is nevertheless forbidden. If one subsequently cooked in it within twenty-four hours a dish that would absorb a beneficial taste from the original forbidden item, the second dish is forbidden if it did not contain sixty times the amount of the original forbidden item. However, if one stirred the first mixture with a spoon and then inserted the spoon into a second mixture to which it would also impart a detrimental taste, then the pot is not forbidden. Similarly, for something that has no taste at all, such as a cauldron in which honey is melted, even if there are bees’ legs in it, the cauldron is not forbidden, and so forth.

And Rav Yehuda says that Shmuel says further: They taught this only with regard to a case where the vinegar fell into hot split beans, as its taste is then detrimental. But if it fell into cold split beans, the vinegar then enhances the taste of the split beans, and even if one subsequently heated them (heated the mixture), it becomes like something that initially enhanced its flavor and ultimately detracted from it, and it is forbidden, because its taste was initially beneficial to them.

Tosafot wondered about the phrase 'it becomes,' since this is indeed the reality being discussed here, that it improves and then ultimately detracts. They answered that the main improvement occurs when one adds the vinegar to them after heating and cooling them (this is how Mahar'am explained it, and so too R. Y. of Paris. See below in Tosefot Chachmei Anglia who did not understand it this way). Similarly, the Ritv'a explained that the intention is not that the split beans literally improve at first, but rather to say that they are not detracted. See also in Chatam Sofer who explained that here it refers to raw split beans on which vinegar fell, which does not detract from their taste, even though they are not yet fit for eating, and therefore it is only 'it becomes like something that enhanced.' Whereas in Tosefot Chachmei Anglia, it was explained that when one eats the split beans in vinegar while they are hot, one reveals their opinion that the vinegar did not initially improve the split beans, and if so, it is not truly an improvement. Simply, 'enhanced and ultimately detracted' should be understood as something that becomes detrimental on its own over time, where there is room to say it is defined as imparting a detrimental flavor, since ultimately it is detrimental. But this case is different, for if one does not heat the split beans, their taste will not be detracted by the vinegar, and if so, this is what is said here 'it becomes,' all the more so that it is forbidden (see Meiri).

The Rambam wrote that the same rule applies if it is detrimental and ultimately beneficial; it is not considered imparting a detrimental flavor, for it is only considered imparting a detrimental flavor if it was so from beginning to end. See in Tosefot Chachmei Anglia who understood that even here, if the split beans cool down after the vinegar fell into them while they were hot, they become improved. He wondered based on this: Why are they not forbidden when the vinegar fell into them, since they are destined to improve when they cool down? He explained that here it refers to someone who eats the split beans while they are hot, and what is said about it imparting a detrimental flavor from beginning to end, means from the time the forbidden item fell until the time of eating. Similarly, the Meiri wrote that a dish that is usually eaten before it cools down is permitted until it cools down. Indeed, from Rashi's words, it implies that from the moment the vinegar fell into the hot split beans, it no longer improves their taste. See in Oraḥ Halakha.

Non-Jewish wine vinegar that fell into hot split beans — it makes them detrimental, and they are permitted. But if it fell into cold split beans, it improves their taste, and they are forbidden even after heating them and it becomes a detrimental flavor. This is in accordance with the words of Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan. (Shulchan Arukh 134:8).

Vinegar that fell on cold split beans, even though they were heated and thereby became detrimental, they are forbidden. This is because what they said, that imparting a detrimental flavor is permitted, applies specifically if it is detrimental from beginning to end. But if it improved and ultimately became detrimental, it is forbidden. The same applies if it was detrimental at first and ultimately improved (specifically after it improved, but while it was still detrimental, it is permitted. Shakh). The commentators disagreed on the law regarding vinegar that fell into hot split beans and then cooled (see Taz and others). (Rambam Sefer Kedusha Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:28. Shulchan Arukh Yoreh De'ah 103:2. See also Shulchan Arukh Yoreh De'ah 98:1).

It becomes like something that enhanced, etc.: It is difficult, why did it use this language, for it certainly enhances? And it can be said that the main enhancement does not occur until after they are heated and cooled.

And similarly, when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia, he reported that Rabba bar bar Ḥana says that Rabbi Yoḥanan says: The Sages taught this only with regard to the case where the vinegar fell into hot split beans. But if the vinegar fell into cold split beans and a person subsequently heated the mixture, it becomes like a dish that some added ingredient first enhanced its flavor and ultimately detracted from it, and it is rendered forbidden. And similarly, when Rav Dimi came, he also reported this in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan and added: And they would prepare this dish of split beans and vinegar on the eves of Shabbat in Tzippori, and they would call it shiḥlayim (cress dish).
And so they would do: They would put vinegar into cold split beans, and it would improve them. And Rav Dimi said this.

And similarly, when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported that Rabba bar bar Ḥana says that Rabbi Yoḥanan says: They taught this only with regard to a case where it fell into hot split beans. But if it fell into cold split beans and one heated them, it becomes like something that initially enhanced its flavor and ultimately detracted from it, and it is forbidden. And similarly, when Rav Dimi came, he said so in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan. And he further added: And they would prepare this with split beans and vinegar on the eves of Shabbat in Tzippori, and they would call them shiḥlayim (a type of cress, used here as a term of praise).

Rabbi Y. of Paris brings in the name of Rashi that after they put vinegar into the cold split beans, they would bury them (which is why Erev Shabbat was mentioned) and the heat would improve them (and so it is brought in Or Zarua in the name of Rashbam that after they put vinegar into the split beans, they would heat them). And he found this difficult, for as stated, heating the split beans with vinegar makes them detrimental. He explained that the intention is that they would soak them for an entire night in vinegar, without burying them. And so in Rashi before us, it is explained that this incident was brought to prove that the vinegar improves the split beans. However, as stated above, some say that the main improvement of the taste in the split beans occurs when they cool down after being heated with vinegar, and it seems that this is how they understood the method of preparation in Tzippori.

And they would call it shiḥlayim: Because they were accustomed to put vinegar in it, just as with shiḥlayim, as we said above regarding (taḥli), if there is vinegar in them, they are spoiled. And Rav Dimi taught us that it was improved by the vinegar.
